title: The Farmer Who Stopped Looking Sideways — A Progressive Movement Disorder That Ended in Status Epilepticus

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 50 years old, a farmer, presenting with frequent falls and walking into objects, drooping eyelids, involuntary hand movements, and talking to himself, all for a year and a half. He completed schooling through the equivalent of high school and is the father of two adult sons. He drank toddy daily and whiskey occasionally, and chewed tobacco several times a day, but stopped both a year before this presentation.

Ten years earlier he had a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure after returning from work, which resolved after receiving fluids at a local hospital. His wife describes him as having previously been an aggressive, quarrelsome person who involved himself in others' affairs.

Two years before this presentation, he had sudden blurred vision while riding his bike, fell, and fractured his left leg, which was surgically repaired; he has had intermittent pus discharge from the surgical site since. During that hospital stay he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on metformin.

Six months after that accident, he began finding it hard to keep his eyes open, worsening through the day and with blinking. He stopped expressing himself emotionally, withdrew from conversation, and began talking and smiling to himself. He started walking into objects and falling, looking only straight ahead without turning his head to the sides, and developed involuntary movements of both hands, especially during work.

Since mid-2020 he has had an intermittent non-productive cough without wheeze, chest pain, or breathlessness. In June 2020 he was found to have a non-healing ulcer at his surgical site, and shortly after had difficulty getting out of bed one morning, leading to a diagnosis of low blood potassium requiring supplementation; this recurred over the following months and required lifelong potassium supplementation. He has been on trihexyphenidyl for the past two months. For the past year he has had a thin urinary stream and nighttime bed-wetting. His serum potassium had been persistently low (2.5–2.9) since June.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General exam:** conscious, coherent, cooperative; pulse 78 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, afebrile; reduced arm swing while walking
- **Cognitive exam:** MMSE score 30/30
- **Motor system:** no muscle wasting; power 5/5 in all four limbs; increased tone throughout; brisk reflexes (3+) at the biceps, triceps, and knees, asymmetric at the ankles (2+ right, 1+ left); flexor plantar responses bilaterally
- **Cranial nerves:** unable to perform upward gaze (third nerve finding); an ice pack test for the ptosis showed no improvement, arguing against myasthenia gravis; all other cranial nerves intact; sensory exam normal
- **Imaging:** CT brain and EEG were both reported as normal
- **X-ray of the left leg:** showed a non-healing fracture, for which removal of the surgical implant was anticipated

**Working diagnosis:** probable progressive supranuclear palsy, in a patient with known type 2 diabetes for two years, meeting NINDS diagnostic criteria after exclusion of other causes.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on levodopa-carbidopa (with the caveat that PSP typically shows minimal or no response to this) and continued metformin, and was discharged on levodopa-carbidopa, metformin, low-dose quetiapine, and an expectorant syrup.

He was readmitted about a week later after an episode of vomiting followed by sweating, rigidity, and disorientation, then a further evening with repeated vomiting and a seizure that brought him to casualty in a stuporous state, with a history of bed-wetting. On arrival his GCS was 3/15, and he had brisk, symmetric reflexes with bilateral extensor plantar responses. He then had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure with tongue-biting and incontinence, followed by a drop in oxygen saturation and a feeble pulse requiring five rounds of CPR; a femoral pulse returned and he was intubated.

He was started on continuous midazolam infusion, nasogastric feeding, pantoprazole, phenytoin, IV fluids, and insulin as needed, with an air bed and two-hourly repositioning, DVT prophylaxis, and frequent glucose, temperature, and sodium monitoring. Over the following days he remained on mechanical ventilation, unconscious, with his working diagnosis expanding to status epilepticus and post-CPR status in addition to his underlying PSP and diabetes. His treatment was adjusted to include 3% hypertonic saline infusion and potassium chloride supplementation once his sodium was found to be low, and antibiotics (augmentin, later ceftriaxone and clindamycin) were added for presumed infection, alongside thiamine supplementation.

A lumbar puncture was performed with cell count and cytology sent. He had further breakthrough seizures over the following days, treated with additional anti-seizure medication, and gradually improved neurologically — his Glasgow Coma Scale rising from 3 to 10 over about ten days — before being extubated. After extubation he continued to have intermittent fever spikes and a few further seizure episodes, managed with ongoing antibiotics, anti-seizure medication, and supportive care, with his diagnosis remaining status epilepticus secondary to hyponatremia, post-CPR status, progressive supranuclear palsy, and type 2 diabetes.
